newsitem.title: USA: Oil up on Iraq, Nigeria tensions, wheat also firm.
newsitem.headline: Oil up on Iraq, Nigeria tensions, wheat also firm.

text.p: Oil prices rose sharply on Monday as political turmoil threatened oil supplies in Nigeria and an Iraqi breach of a "no-fly" zone threatened that country's oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.

In other markets, wheat prices rose on crop worries and pork belly prices soared on strong export demand. The Commodity Research Bureau's index of 17 futures contracts closed 0.27 point higher at 247.61.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil for May delivery rose 47 cents a barrel to close at $20.38. Buoyed by the gains, May heating oil closed 0.80 cent a gallon higher at 55.48 cents and May gasoline rose 1.31 cents to 62.80 cents.

Iraq said on Monday it would send helicopters to pick up returning Moslem pilgrims at the Saudi Arabian border despite a ban by the United States and other Western powers on Iraqi flights in the area.
The White House on Monday told Iraq to reconsider its decision and said it would "respond appropriately" but would not shoot down civilian helicopters.
"The Iraqis are in no position to give any kind of dictates to the American people or to NATO or to the United Nations," Defense Secretary William Cohen said.
When Iraq flew the pilgrims on April 9 to Mecca for the haj pilgrimage, the U.N. Security Council issued a statement calling on Iraq not to fly more planes without its consent.

"Since the U.S. has said they would respond, the market thinks it could ask the U.N. not to renew the oil-for-food deal," said Ed Kevelson, director of refined products for Paribas Futures Inc in New York.
Under last year's accord, the United Nations eased sanctions against Iraq and allowed Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months on a renewable basis to buy food and humanitarian supplies.

Meanwhile, in Nigeria the Royal Dutch/Shell Group said it had closed one facility and production was running 2,000 barrels per day below normal because of renewed ethnic clashes in the oil-producing area of Warri.
Tribal clashes in the oil exporting nation occurred in March when armed Ijaw tribesmen occupied six Shell facilities. Market players said they were concerned the exports could again be affected.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat prices closed higher as traders continued to worry about freeze damage to the winter wheat crop, flooding delays for spring wheat and persistent dryness in Europe that may shrink the crop there.
Wheat for delivery in May at the Chicago Board of Trade rose 2-1/2 cents a bushel to close at $4.39-1/2, its highest closing price since August 13.

"Flooding in the Northern Plains is very bad and there was very little relief in Europe over the weekend," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter. "There was a little rain in southern France but not much, and the forecasts are dry."

North Dakota Congressman Earl Pomeroy said on Sunday about 1.7 million acres of North Dakota cropland were under water from flooding and snowmelt and much of that acreage will not go into agricultural production this growing season.
North Dakota, especially the Red River Valley region between North Dakota and Minnesota, is a key region that produces spring wheat and sugar beets.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, pork belly futures set new life-of-contract highs across the board as optimism about future export demand to Asia following last month's halt of Taiwan's pork exports overcame a rise in reported supply.
Pork bellies for May delivery closed up 1.45 cents a pound at 91.40 cents.
A monthly report on Friday from the Agriculture Department reported stocks of frozen bellies at 54.8 million pounds at the end of March, higher than most analysts had expected.
But demand remains evident from increased export demand for bellies, light weekly storings during April and an expected slowdown in the rate of hog slaughter, traders said.
"The Japanese situation, having them come in and buy, is the major reason for this rally," said Dan Vaught, livestock analyst for brokerage AG Edwards.

Japan said last week that it would buy U.S. pork bellies until late May to supplement needs through the end of the year because of a ban on Taiwan pork exports following an epidemic of foot-and-mouth disease in Taiwan's hog herd.
